On the Limits of Latent Reuse in Diffusion Models

Yifeng Yu Thanks: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University yyf22@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Lu Yu Thanks:  Department of Data Science, City University of Hong Kong lu.yu@cityu.edu.hk
Abstract

Diffusion models are often trained in low-dimensional latent spaces, which are then reused for related but shifted datasets. In this work, we study when such latent reuse remains reliable under distribution shift. We consider a source-target setting in which both datasets are approximately low-dimensional but may lie near different subspaces. We show that freezing and reusing a source latent space induces a target-domain score error governed by two quantities: the principal-angle misalignment between the source and target subspaces, and the target ambient noise amplified by the diffusion time scale. Motivated by these limits, we further study mixed source-target training and characterize how the required shared latent dimension depends on the relative geometry of the two distributions. Our results provide theoretical guidance on when latent reuse is reliable and when learning a shared representation may be necessary.

1 Introduction

Diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable breakthroughs across multiple domains [RDN+22, PVG+21, XYS+22]. Their success is driven by a denoising principle: a forward process gradually corrupts data with Gaussian noise, while a learned score function is used to reverse this process and generate new samples [SSDK+20]. In many modern applications, however, diffusion models are not trained directly in the original ambient space. Instead, high-dimensional data such as high-resolution images are first compressed by an encoder, often the encoder of a variational autoencoder (VAE), and the diffusion model is trained in the resulting lower-dimensional latent space [RBL+22, PEL+23, CYG+23, CGX+24, WZL+25]. This strategy is computationally attractive and is consistent with the empirical observation that many high-dimensional datasets exhibit strong low-dimensional structure [PZA+21]. After pretraining, the representation map is often kept fixed and reused for related datasets, while a new score model is trained in the induced latent coordinates [CYG+23, CGX+24, LSH+25, WZL+25].

While convenient, latent reuse raises a fundamental question: when does a latent space learned from a source distribution remain reliable under target shift? The answer is not obvious, since a representation that is effective for the source distribution need not preserve all directions relevant to the target score.

Existing theory provides important insight into why diffusion models can exploit low-dimensional structure. A growing line of work establishes score approximation, score estimation, and distribution recovery guarantees when the data lie on, or near, an unknown low-dimensional subspace or manifold, with rates depending primarily on the intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension [CHZW23, LY24, WZZ+25, HWL+24, OAS23, ADR24, TY24, CXXZ25, YP25, LHC25, HWC26, AVS+24]. These results, however, are largely single-distribution in nature: they explain the benefits of low-dimensional modeling, while leaving open how a learned representation behaves when reused under distribution shift.

A separate line of work studies transfer and adaptation of diffusion models across domains [CXZZ25, OXZC24, SMHL25, KBK+25, MCL+22, XYS+23, HLZ+23]. For example, recent work represents the target-domain score through a pretrained source-domain score together with additional guidance [OXZC24, KBK+25], while other work establishes sample-efficient transfer guarantees for conditional diffusion models through the lens of representation learning [CXZZ25]. These works show how pretrained diffusion models or learned representations can be adapted across related tasks. Complementary to this perspective, we study a different widely used practice: freezing a data latent space learned from a source distribution and reusing it as the coordinate system for score estimation on a shifted target distribution. This distinction is important because latent reuse can fail for reasons that are invisible in existing single-distribution low-dimensional theory. Even when both source and target distributions are approximately low-dimensional, the source latent space may be poorly aligned with the target signal subspace, and the target distribution may contain ambient noise outside the reused representation. In this case, no downstream score model trained only on the reused latent coordinates can fully recover the missing target directions.

Motivated by this gap, we take a first step toward a mathematical understanding of latent reuse under source-target distribution shift. We consider a model where both distributions are approximately low-dimensional but may concentrate near different subspaces, allowing us to isolate how representation mismatch affects score estimation. Our analysis shows that frozen reuse can fail for geometric reasons that cannot be resolved solely by more target samples or a more expressive downstream score model. This motivates mixed source–target training as an alternative strategy for learning a shared representation adapted to both distributions. Towards this, our contributions can be summarized as follows.

  • •

    Identifying the limits of frozen latent reuse. In Theorem 2, we show that frozen reuse can incur irreducible target-domain score error, even with an arbitrarily expressive downstream score model. The bound identifies two concrete failure mechanisms: principal-angle misalignment with the target subspace and target ambient noise amplified by the diffusion time scale.

  • •

    Quantifying when frozen reuse is reliable. In Proposition 3 and Theorem 5, we construct an explicit frozen-coordinate comparator and derive a finite-sample ReLU score-estimation guarantee. These results separate statistical, approximation, and geometric errors, thereby clarifying when the cost of latent reuse is small and when it remains intrinsic.

  • •

    Mixed training beyond frozen reuse. In Proposition 6, Theorem 7, and Corollary 8, we analyze mixed source–target training through a shared-projector oracle. The results show how learning a shared representation can reduce, and in favorable containment regimes remove, the target signal-mismatch term that persists under source-aligned reuse.

Overall, our results suggest that latent reuse should be viewed not only as a downstream score-estimation problem, but also as a representation-level constraint governed by the relative geometry of the source and target low-dimensional structures. In particular, the bounds show that low-dimensionality alone does not guarantee reliable reuse: alignment, latent dimension, and ambient-noise effects all influence the resulting score error. These observations provide a step toward a more precise theoretical understanding of when frozen latent reuse is appropriate and when learning a shared representation may be beneficial.

2 Preliminaries

We begin by introducing the diffusion model used throughout the paper, followed by the source-target setting in which latent representations are learned, frozen, and reused under distribution shift.

2.1 Diffusion Models

Framework. We consider the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck forward process

d​Xt=−12​Xt​d​t+d​Wt,t∈[0,T],\displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}X_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t},\qquad t\in[0,T], (2.1)

where the initial point X0∼p0X_{0}\sim p_{0} follow an unknown data distribution p0p_{0}, and WtW_{t} denotes a standard DD-dimensional Brownian motion. This process admits the explicit transition kernel

Xt|X0∼𝒩⁡(α⁡(t)​X0,h⁡(t)​ID),\displaystyle X_{t}\mid X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\alpha(t)X_{0},h(t)I_{D}\bigr), (2.2)

with α(t)=e−t/2,h(t)=1−e−t.\alpha(t)=e^{-t/2},h(t)=1-e^{-t}. Thus, the marginal density of XtX_{t} is

pt​(x)=∫ℝD𝒩⁡(x,α⁡(t)​x0,h⁡(t)​ID)​p0​(x0)​d​x0.\displaystyle p_{t}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{D}}\mathcal{N}\bigl(x;\alpha(t)x_{0},h(t)I_{D}\bigr)p_{0}(x_{0})\,\mathrm{d}x_{0}. (2.3)

Sampling from p0p_{0} can be performed by reversing the noising process [And82, CCGL23]. The corresponding reverse-time SDE is

dXt←=[12X←t+∇xlogpT−t(X←t)]dt+dW¯t,\displaystyle\mathrm{d}X^{\leftarrow}_{t}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\frac{1}{2}X^{\leftarrow}_{t}+\nabla_{x}\log p_{T-t}\bigl(X^{\leftarrow}_{t}\bigr)}}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}\bar{W}_{t}, (2.4)

where W¯t\bar{W}_{t} is a standard Brownian motion, independent of WtW_{t}. The vector field ∇x​log​pt​(x)\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(x) is called the score function for ptp_{t}. It is typically unknown, since ptp_{t} is not available in closed form.

Score Matching. In practice, one trains a parametrized score network sθ​(x,t)s_{\theta}(x,t) to approximate ∇x​log​pt​(x)\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(x), typically through an L2L^{2} score-matching objective of the form

minimizeθ∈Θ𝔼[∥sθ(Xt,t)−∇xlogpt(Xt)∥22].\displaystyle\underset{\theta\in\Theta}{\text{minimize}}~~~\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\bigl\|s_{\theta}(X_{t},t)-\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(X_{t})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}}}\right]. (2.5)

Substituting the learned score estimate into the reverse process (2.4) yields the practical continuous-time backward SDE, which is typically approximated by a discretization method (e.g. [YY26, CLL23, DB22]).

2.2 Source-target Setting

In this work, we study latent reuse in a source-target setting. The source distribution p1p_{1} represents the distribution used to learn the latent representation, while the target distribution p2p_{2} represents the shifted distribution on which this representation is reused. We assume that both distributions are approximately low-dimensional, with each lying near a possibly different linear subspace and perturbed by isotropic ambient noise.

Assumption 1.

For each domain i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, a data point x∼pix\sim p_{i} is generated via

x=Ai​zi+εi,x=A_{i}z_{i}+\varepsilon_{i},

where Ai∈ℝD×diA_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{i}} has orthonormal columns, i.e., Ai⊤​Ai=IdiA_{i}^{\top}A_{i}=I_{d_{i}}, zi∼pi,zz_{i}\sim p_{i,z} is a latent variable in ℝdi\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}, and the ambient noise εi∼𝒩⁡(0,σi2​ID)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{i}^{2}I_{D}) is independent of ziz_{i}, with σi>0\sigma_{i}>0.

Assumption 1 extends the exact linear-subspace model commonly used in low-dimensional diffusion theory [CHZW23, HWL+24, YJC+24] by allowing isotropic ambient noise. Here, Ai​ziA_{i}z_{i} represents the intrinsic low-dimensional signal, while εi\varepsilon_{i} captures deviations from col⁡(Ai)\operatorname{col}(A_{i}). The source and target subspaces are unknown and may differ, allowing us to quantify the effect of latent reuse through subspace misalignment and target ambient noise.

Under this model, Gaussian noising yields an explicit score decomposition.

3 Main Results

We now present our main theoretical results. Section 3.1 analyzes frozen latent reuse on the target distribution and identifies the structural bias induced by subspace mismatch and target ambient noise. Section 3.2 complements this with an explicit comparator and a finite-sample bound for target-domain training with a frozen projector. Finally, Section 3.3 studies mixed source-target training as an alternative to frozen reuse.

3.1 Irreducible Error under Frozen Latent Reuse

We first identify a structural limitation of frozen latent reuse: even if the downstream score model is arbitrarily expressive, a fixed source latent space may leave irreducible target-domain error.

The first term captures target signal directions missed by the frozen source subspace, and it vanishes when col⁡(A2)⊆col⁡(V1)\operatorname{col}(A_{2})\subseteq\operatorname{col}(V_{1}). The second term captures target ambient noise outside the frozen output subspace, amplified by the diffusion time scale. Thus, the lower bound identifies a genuine limit of latent reuse: even an arbitrarily expressive core map cannot recover target score components that are absent from the frozen coordinates.

3.2 Achievability and Statistical Error under Frozen Reuse

The preceding lower bound identifies regimes in which frozen reuse incurs intrinsic error. We next complement this result by studying what can be achieved when the frozen subspace is sufficiently aligned with the target distribution. To this end, we introduce an explicit frozen-coordinate comparator and derive the corresponding statistical guarantee.

To establish the bounds, we require mild regularity of the target latent distribution and its induced score map.

Assumption 2.

The target latent density p2,z>0p_{2,z}>0 is twice continuously differentiable. Moreover, there exist constants B2,C1,2,C2,2>0B_{2},C_{1,2},C_{2,2}>0 such that, for all ‖z‖2⩾B2\|z\|_{2}\geqslant B_{2}, it holds that

The target core score map f2∗(z,t):=h~2(t)∇logp2,tLD(z)+zf_{2}^{*}(z,t):=\widetilde{h}_{2}(t)\nabla\log p_{2,t}^{\rm LD}(z)+z is uniformly β2\beta_{2}-Lipschitz in z∈ℝd2z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}} for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

𝒰comp​(V1)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1}) ⩽1T−t0∫t0T[λg,2max​(t)h2​(t)(d2−∑j=1d1cos2⁡θjCLOSE)+2​‖B‖op2​Lg2​(t)h2​(t)Tr((Id2−B†​B)​MY,2​(t)CLOSE)\displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{T-t_{0}}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\Bigg[\frac{\lambda_{g,2}^{\max}(t)}{h^{2}(t)}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(d_{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{d_{1}}\cos^{2}\theta_{j}}}\right)+\frac{2\|B\|_{\rm op}^{2}L_{g}^{2}(t)}{h^{2}(t)}\operatorname{Tr}\!\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left((I_{d_{2}}-B^{\dagger}B)M_{Y,2}(t)}}\right)
+2​‖B‖op2​h~2​(t)​Lg2​(t)h2​(t)∑j=1d1tan2θj+σ24​α4​(t)h2​(t)​h~2​(t)(D+d1−d2−∑j=1d1cos2⁡θjCLOSE)]dt.\displaystyle+\frac{2\|B\|_{\rm op}^{2}\widetilde{h}_{2}(t)L_{g}^{2}(t)}{h^{2}(t)}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{1}}\tan^{2}\theta_{j}+\frac{\sigma_{2}^{4}\alpha^{4}(t)}{h^{2}(t)\widetilde{h}_{2}(t)}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(D+d_{1}-d_{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{d_{1}}\cos^{2}\theta_{j}}}\right)\Bigg]\mathrm{d}t.

When d1⩾d2d_{1}\geqslant d_{2}, the frozen space has sufficient dimension to represent the target subspace, and the main difficulty is stability, as reflected by tan2⁡θj\tan^{2}\theta_{j}. When d1<d2d_{1}<d_{2}, the frozen space is dimensionally insufficient, leading to the additional information-loss term OPENTr⁡((Id2−B†​B)​MY,2​(t)CLOSE)\operatorname{Tr}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left((I_{d_{2}}-B^{\dagger}B)M_{Y,2}(t)}}\right) in addition to the output-side residual d2−∑j=1d1cos2⁡θjd_{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{d_{1}}\cos^{2}\theta_{j}. Thus, frozen reuse can fail either because the reused space is poorly aligned with the target subspace, or because it is too small to contain the target-relevant directions.

We now connect the measurable comparator bound to the practical ReLU estimator. The argument has two steps. First, the frozen ReLU oracle risk is controlled by the measurable comparator risk plus the cost of approximating the comparator within the ReLU class. Second, the empirical denoising-risk minimizer is controlled by this frozen oracle risk up to a finite-sample error.

Recall that ℬfreeze​(V1):=infs∈𝒮freeze​(V1)ℒ2​(s)\mathcal{B}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1}):=\inf_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})}\mathcal{L}_{2}(s) is the population oracle risk over the frozen ReLU class. To pass from the measurable comparator to this class, define

𝒜comp(fθ;V1):=1T−t0∫t0T1h2​(t)𝔼Xt∼p2,t[∥fθ(V1⊤Xt,t)−fcomp(V1⊤Xt,t)∥22]dt.\mathcal{A}_{\rm comp}(f_{\theta};V_{1}):=\frac{1}{T-t_{0}}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\frac{1}{h^{2}(t)}\mathbb{E}_{X_{t}\sim p_{2,t}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\|f_{\theta}(V_{1}^{\top}X_{t},t)-f_{\rm comp}(V_{1}^{\top}X_{t},t)\|_{2}^{2}}}\right]\,\mathrm{d}t.

This term measures the approximation error incurred by replacing the measurable comparator fcompf_{\rm comp} with a ReLU network on the frozen-coordinate distribution.

Lemma 4 (Comparator-to-ReLU transfer).

Let

scomp​(x,t):=1h⁡(t)​V1​fcomp​(V1⊤​x,t)−1h⁡(t)​x,\displaystyle s_{\rm comp}(x,t):=\frac{1}{h(t)}V_{1}f_{\rm comp}(V_{1}^{\top}x,t)-\frac{1}{h(t)}x,

and let 𝒰comp​(V1):=ℒ2​(scomp)\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1}):=\mathcal{L}_{2}(s_{\rm comp}). Then, for any η>0\eta>0,

OPENℬfreeze​(V1)⩽(1+η)​𝒰comp​(V1)+(1+1ηCLOSE)​inffθ∈ℱReLU(d1)𝒜comp​(fθ,V1).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})\leqslant(1+\eta)\,\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1})+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\frac{1}{\eta}}}\right)\inf_{f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm ReLU}^{(d_{1})}}\mathcal{A}_{\rm comp}(f_{\theta};V_{1}).

By Lemma 4, for any η>0\eta>0,

OPENℬfreeze​(V1)≤(1+η)​𝒰comp​(V1)+(1+1ηCLOSE)​inffθ∈ℱReLU(d1)𝒜comp​(fθ,V1).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})\leq(1+\eta)\,\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1})+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\frac{1}{\eta}}}\right)\inf_{f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm ReLU}^{(d_{1})}}\mathcal{A}_{\rm comp}(f_{\theta};V_{1}). (3.1)

Thus, the frozen ReLU oracle risk is controlled by the geometry-dependent comparator error and the ReLU approximation error for fcompf_{\rm comp}.

We next pass from the frozen oracle risk to finite-sample training. Let x1,…,xN2x_{1},\ldots,x_{N_{2}} be i.i.d. samples from p2p_{2}. For any score network ss, define the target-domain denoising loss

ℓ2(x;s):=1T−t0∫t0T𝔼Xt∼p2,t(⋅∣X0=x)[‖∇Xtlogϕt(Xt∣x)−s(Xt,t)‖22]dt,\ell_{2}(x;s):=\frac{1}{T-t_{0}}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{X_{t}\sim p_{2,t}(\cdot\mid X_{0}=x)}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\nabla_{X_{t}}\log\phi_{t}(X_{t}\mid x)-s(X_{t},t)}}\right\|_{2}^{2}}}\right]\,\mathrm{d}t,

where ϕt(⋅∣x)\phi_{t}(\cdot\mid x) denotes the Gaussian transition density of XtX_{t} conditional on X0=xX_{0}=x. Define

ℛ2​(s):=𝔼X0∼p2​[ℓ2​(X0,s)],ℛ^2​(s):=1N2​∑i=1N2ℓ2​(xi,s),\mathcal{R}_{2}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{X_{0}\sim p_{2}}[\ell_{2}(X_{0};s)],\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{2}(s):=\frac{1}{N_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{2}}\ell_{2}(x_{i};s),

and let

s^freeze∈⁡a​r​g​m​i​ns∈𝒮freeze​(V1)​ℛ^2​(s).\widehat{s}_{\rm freeze}\in\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{2}(s).

Although s^freeze\widehat{s}_{\rm freeze} is trained by minimizing the empirical denoising risk, our target quantity is the population score error ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2}. The denoising score-matching identity implies that there exists a constant E2E_{2}, independent of ss, such that

ℛ2​(s)=ℒ2​(s)+E2.\mathcal{R}_{2}(s)=\mathcal{L}_{2}(s)+E_{2}.

The identity between the denoising objective and score matching follows from the denoising score matching argument of Vincent [Vin11]. Therefore, population minimization of ℛ2\mathcal{R}_{2} is equivalent to population minimization of ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2}. Moreover, if

StatErrN2:=2sups∈𝒮freeze​(V1)|ℛ^2(s)−ℛ2(s)|,\mathrm{StatErr}_{N_{2}}:=2\sup_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{2}(s)-\mathcal{R}_{2}(s)}}\right|,

then the empirical minimizer satisfies the oracle inequality

ℒ2​(s^freeze)⩽ℬfreeze​(V1)+StatErrN2.\mathcal{L}_{2}(\widehat{s}_{\rm freeze})\leqslant\mathcal{B}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})+\mathrm{StatErr}_{N_{2}}.

Combining this inequality with the comparator decomposition in (3.1) gives the following bound.

Theorem 5.

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, and 3 hold for p2p_{2}. Let V1∈ℝD×d1V_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{1}} be fixed independently of the target samples, with V1⊤​V1=Id1V_{1}^{\top}V_{1}=I_{d_{1}}. For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), set

Rz=Cz(1+σ2)(d2+log⁡8​N2δCLOSE),R⟂=C⟂σ2(D−d2+log⁡8​N2δCLOSE),R_{z}=C_{z}(1+\sigma_{2})\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sqrt{d_{2}}+\sqrt{\log\frac{8N_{2}}{\delta}}}}\right),\qquad R_{\perp}=C_{\perp}\sigma_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sqrt{D-d_{2}}+\sqrt{\log\frac{8N_{2}}{\delta}}}}\right),

and define

𝒯2(Rz,R⟂):={x∈ℝD:∥A2⊤x∥2≤Rz,∥P2⟂x∥2≤R⟂}.\mathcal{T}_{2}(R_{z},R_{\perp}):=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}:\|A_{2}^{\top}x\|_{2}\leq R_{z},\ \|P_{2}^{\perp}x\|_{2}\leq R_{\perp}}}\right\}.

For ι>0\iota>0, let

𝒩2(ι):=𝒩(ι,{ℓ2(⋅;s)𝟏𝒯2​(Rz,R⟂)(⋅):s∈𝒮freeze(V1)},∥⋅∥∞).\mathcal{N}_{2}(\iota):=\mathcal{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\iota,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\ell_{2}(\cdot;s)\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{T}_{2}(R_{z},R_{\perp})}(\cdot):s\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm freeze}(V_{1})}}\right\},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}}}\right).

If the ReLU architecture is chosen so that

inffθ∈ℱReLU(d1)𝒜comp​(fθ,V1)≲(d1+1)​ϵ2t0​(T−t0),\inf_{f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm ReLU}^{(d_{1})}}\mathcal{A}_{\rm comp}(f_{\theta};V_{1})\lesssim\frac{(d_{1}+1)\epsilon^{2}}{t_{0}(T-t_{0})},

then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, it holds that

ℒ2(s^freeze)⩽𝒪~(K2+Rz2+R⟂2N2​t0​(T−t0)​ϵ2[log𝒩2(ι)+log8δ]+ι)+𝒪((d1+1)​ϵ2t0​(T−t0)CLOSE)+𝒪(𝒰comp​(V1)CLOSE).\mathcal{L}_{2}(\widehat{s}_{\rm freeze})\leqslant\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{K^{2}+R_{z}^{2}+R_{\perp}^{2}}{N_{2}t_{0}(T-t_{0})\epsilon^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\log\mathcal{N}_{2}(\iota)+\log\frac{8}{\delta}}}\right]+\iota}}\right)+\mathcal{O}\!\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{(d_{1}+1)\epsilon^{2}}{t_{0}(T-t_{0})}}}\right)+\mathcal{O}\!\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1})}}\right).

Here, KK is the uniform output bound of the ReLU network class, and Cz,C⟂C_{z},C_{\perp} depend only on the target latent tail constants and absolute Gaussian concentration constants.

The bound decomposes the target-domain error into three terms: finite-sample estimation error, ReLU approximation error, and the geometry-dependent comparator error 𝒰comp​(V1)\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1}). The first term decreases as the number N2N_{2} of target samples increases, and the second term can be reduced by enlarging the ReLU class. In contrast, 𝒰comp​(V1)\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1}) is determined by the compatibility between the frozen representation and the target distribution, as quantified in Proposition 3.

This reveals a fundamental limitation of latent reuse. If the frozen subspace is not well aligned with the target subspace, or if its dimension is too small to contain the target-relevant directions, then the geometric term 𝒰comp​(V1)\mathcal{U}_{\rm comp}(V_{1}) may remain large. In this case, latent reuse can fail even with many target samples and an expressive downstream score network, because the relevant target information has already been lost or distorted by the frozen representation. This motivates a different strategy: rather than reusing a fixed source representation, we train on mixed source–target data so that the learned representation can better reflect the target-domain structure.

3.3 Mixed Source-target Training

In this section, we study this idea at the oracle level by comparing two fixed projectors: the frozen source projector V1V_{1} and a newly learned shared projector WkW_{k} of dimension kk. Let

pmix:=ω1​p1+ω2​p2,p_{\rm mix}:=\omega_{1}p_{1}+\omega_{2}p_{2},

where ω1,ω2>0\omega_{1},\omega_{2}>0 and ω1+ω2=1\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}=1. For a kk-dimensional projector W∈ℝD×kW\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times k} and weights c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0, define the weighted signal residual

Γk​(W):=ω1​c1​‖PW⟂​A1‖F2+ω2​c2​‖PW⟂​A2‖F2.\Gamma_{k}(W):=\omega_{1}c_{1}\|P_{W}^{\perp}A_{1}\|_{F}^{2}+\omega_{2}c_{2}\|P_{W}^{\perp}A_{2}\|_{F}^{2}\,.

Proposition 6.

Let Ai∈ℝD×diA_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{i}} have orthonormal columns, and constants c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0. Then, for any k∈{max⁡(d1,d2),…,D}k\in\{\max(d_{1},d_{2}),\ldots,D\}, it holds that

infW:W⊤​W=IkΓk(W)=Tr(Mmix)−∑j=1kλj(Mmix)=∑j=k+1Dλj(Mmix).\inf_{W:W^{\top}W=I_{k}}\Gamma_{k}(W)=\operatorname{Tr}(M_{\rm mix})-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}(M_{\rm mix})=\sum_{j=k+1}^{D}\lambda_{j}(M_{\rm mix}).

The infimum is attained by any WkW_{k} whose columns span a top-kk eigenspace of MmixM_{\rm mix}. In particular, the optimal residual is nonincreasing in kk and vanishes if span⁡(A1)+span⁡(A2)⊆span⁡(Wk).\operatorname{span}(A_{1})+\operatorname{span}(A_{2})\subseteq\operatorname{span}(W_{k}).

Proposition 6 gives a simple geometric reason to retrain a shared latent space. If the frozen source projector V1V_{1} misses target directions, then WkW_{k} minimizes the joint source–target signal residual among all kk-dimensional projectors. When WkW_{k} contains the union of the source and target signal subspaces, this signal-side residual is completely removed.

We next connect the geometric improvement of the mixed projector to the mixed score-oracle error. For a fixed orthonormal projector U∈ℝD×mU\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times m}, with U=V1U=V_{1} or U=WkU=W_{k}, define

ℬmix​(U):=infs∈𝒮mix​(U)ℒmix​(s),\mathcal{B}_{\rm mix}(U):=\inf_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm mix}(U)}\mathcal{L}_{\rm mix}(s),

where

𝒮mix(U):={sU,θ(x,t)=1h⁡(t)Ufθ(U⊤x,t)−1h⁡(t)x:fθ∈ℱReLU(m)}\mathcal{S}_{\rm mix}(U):=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s_{U,\theta}(x,t)=\frac{1}{h(t)}Uf_{\theta}(U^{\top}x,t)-\frac{1}{h(t)}x:f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm ReLU}^{(m)}}}\right\}

is the score class using the projected coordinates U⊤​xU^{\top}x, and ℒmix\mathcal{L}_{\rm mix} denotes the integrated score risk under pmixp_{\rm mix}:

ℒmix(s):=1T−t0∫t0T𝔼Xt∼pmix,t[∥s(Xt,t)−∇logpmix,t(Xt)∥22]dt.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm mix}(s):=\frac{1}{T-t_{0}}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{X_{t}\sim p_{{\rm mix},t}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\|s(X_{t},t)-\nabla\log p_{{\rm mix},t}(X_{t})\|_{2}^{2}}}\right]\,\mathrm{d}t.

Theorem 7.

Suppose Assumption 1 and 3 hold for both p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}, together with the regularity assumptions required for the mixed comparators, whose precise statement is deferred to Appendix C.3. Let WkW_{k} be the optimizer in Proposition 6 with ci=c¯ic_{i}=\bar{c}_{i}. Then, for U∈{V1,Wk}U\in\{V_{1},W_{k}\} and any η>0\eta>0,

ℬmix​(U)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\rm mix}(U) ⩽(1+η)​[Γ⁡(U)+∑i=12ωi​n¯i​Tr⁡(PU⟂​Pi⟂)+2​∑i=12ωi​ℜi​(U)+2​𝔓​(U)]\displaystyle\leqslant(1+\eta)\Bigg[\Gamma(U)+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\omega_{i}\bar{n}_{i}\operatorname{Tr}(P_{U}^{\perp}P_{i}^{\perp})+2\sum_{i=1}^{2}\omega_{i}\mathfrak{R}_{i}(U)+2\mathfrak{P}(U)\Bigg]

Theorem 7 separates the mixed oracle risk into a leading signal-residual term, an ambient-noise term, reconstruction ℜi​(U)\mathfrak{R}_{i}(U) and posterior-compression terms 𝔓⁡(U)\mathfrak{P}(U). The auxiliary quantities ℜi​(U)\mathfrak{R}_{i}(U) and 𝔓⁡(U)\mathfrak{P}(U) capture, respectively, the componentwise reconstruction error from the projected coordinates U⊤​xU^{\top}x and the loss of mixture-component information after projection. Their explicit forms, together with the full mixed oracle decomposition, are given in Appendix C.3.

The leading projector-dependent term in the upper bound of Theorem 7 is Γ⁡(U)\Gamma(U). Since Mmix=∑i=12ωi​c¯i​Ai​Ai⊤,M_{\rm mix}=\sum_{i=1}^{2}\omega_{i}\bar{c}_{i}A_{i}A_{i}^{\top}, Proposition 6 implies that the optimal kk-dimensional mixed projector WkW_{k} satisfies Γ⁡(Wk)=∑j=k+1Dλj​(Mmix).\Gamma(W_{k})=\sum_{j=k+1}^{D}\lambda_{j}(M_{\rm mix}). Thus, compared with frozen reuse, the shared projector WkW_{k} reduces the leading signal residual by

Γ⁡(V1)−Γ⁡(Wk)=Γ⁡(V1)−∑j=k+1Dλj​(Mmix).\Gamma(V_{1})-\Gamma(W_{k})=\Gamma(V_{1})-\sum_{j=k+1}^{D}\lambda_{j}(M_{\rm mix}).

Thus, mixed training improves the oracle upper bound when this reduction dominates the corresponding changes in the ambient-noise, reconstruction, posterior-compression, and ReLU approximation terms. The following corollary illustrates the most favorable case, where the mixed projector contains both source and target signal subspaces.

Corollary 8.

Suppose WkW_{k} satisfies span⁡(A1)+span⁡(A2)⊆span⁡(Wk).\operatorname{span}(A_{1})+\operatorname{span}(A_{2})\subseteq\operatorname{span}(W_{k}). Then, for any η>0\eta>0,

ℬmix​(Wk)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\rm mix}(W_{k}) ⩽(1+η)[∑i=12ωin¯i(D−k)+2∑i=12ωin¯i(k−di)+2𝔓(Wk)]\displaystyle\leqslant(1+\eta)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\omega_{i}\bar{n}_{i}(D-k)+2\sum_{i=1}^{2}\omega_{i}\bar{n}_{i}(k-d_{i})+2\mathfrak{P}(W_{k})}}\right]
OPEN+(1+1ηCLOSE)​inffθ∈ℱReLU(k)𝒜mix​(fθ,Wk),\displaystyle+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\frac{1}{\eta}}}\right)\inf_{f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm ReLU}^{(k)}}\mathcal{A}_{\rm mix}(f_{\theta};W_{k})\,,

where n¯i:=1T−t0​∫t0Tα4​(t)​σi4h2​(t)​h~i​(t)​𝑑t\bar{n}_{i}:=\frac{1}{T-t_{0}}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\frac{\alpha^{4}(t)\sigma_{i}^{4}}{h^{2}(t)\tilde{h}_{i}(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t. In particular, if V1=A1V_{1}=A_{1}, then

Γ⁡(V1)=ω2​c¯2​‖PA1⟂​A2‖F2,Γ⁡(Wk)=0.\Gamma(V_{1})=\omega_{2}\bar{c}_{2}\|P_{A_{1}}^{\perp}A_{2}\|_{F}^{2},\qquad\Gamma(W_{k})=0.

Thus, in the containment regime, mixed training removes the target signal-mismatch term that remains under source-aligned reuse.

The posterior-compression term 𝔓⁡(Wk)\mathfrak{P}(W_{k}) does not necessarily vanish under the containment condition alone. It vanishes under the stronger condition that the projected coordinate Wk⊤​XtW_{k}^{\top}X_{t} is sufficient for identifying the mixture component. For instance, this holds when WkW_{k} contains both signal subspaces and the two mixture components have identical ambient-noise distributions. In this case, mixed training eliminates the source–target signal-mismatch term, leaving only ambient-noise, reconstruction, and ReLU approximation contributions.

4 Discussion

Our analysis focuses on a noisy linear low-dimensional model, where the source and target distributions concentrate near possibly different subspaces. This setting makes the geometric obstruction to latent reuse explicit through principal angles and ambient-noise terms, but it does not capture the nonlinear latent representations often used in practice. A natural next step is to extend the theory to nonlinear low-dimensional structures, such as distributions supported near smooth manifolds, as studied for example in [ADR24, YP25, TY24]. In such settings, subspace mismatch would be replaced by tangent-space mismatch and curvature effects.

Another limitation is that our mixed-training analysis is carried out at the oracle level, treating the shared projector as fixed once chosen. This isolates the representation-level mechanism, but does not account for the finite-sample cost of learning the projector from mixed data. A more complete theory would combine representation learning error, score-estimation error, and sampling error in a single end-to-end guarantee. It would also be interesting to study adaptive mixtures, where the relative amount of source and target data is chosen according to the degree of distribution shift.

Appendix B Proof of Auxiliary Lemmas

Proof. [Proof of Lemma 1] The proof follows the exact orthogonal decomposition framework as Lemma 1 in [CHZW23], with one crucial algebraic modification regarding the transition kernel.

Under our Assumption 1, the initial data incorporates ambient noise X0=Ai​z+ϵiX_{0}=A_{i}z+\epsilon_{i}, where ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,σi2​ID)\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{i}^{2}I_{D}). By the convolution of independent Gaussian distributions, the conditional transition kernel of the forward diffusion process becomes Xt|z∼𝒩⁡(α⁡(t)​Ai​z,h~i​(t)​ID)X_{t}|z\sim\mathcal{N}(\alpha(t)A_{i}z,\tilde{h}_{i}(t)I_{D}), where the effective variance is strictly h~i​(t)=α2​(t)​σi2+h⁡(t)\tilde{h}_{i}(t)=\alpha^{2}(t)\sigma_{i}^{2}+h(t).

Substituting this effective variance h~i​(t)\tilde{h}_{i}(t) for the pure diffusion variance h⁡(t)h(t) in the spatial Pythagorean decomposition (i.e., ‖x−α⁡(t)​Ai​z‖22=‖Ai⊤​x−α⁡(t)​z‖22+‖(ID−Ai​Ai⊤)​x‖22\|x-\alpha(t)A_{i}z\|_{2}^{2}=\|A_{i}^{\top}x-\alpha(t)z\|_{2}^{2}+\|(I_{D}-A_{i}A_{i}^{\top})x\|_{2}^{2}) directly yields the stated factorization of the marginal density and the corresponding score function. ∎

Lemma 9.

Let F:ℝm×[t0,T]→ℝmF:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times[t_{0},T]\to\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfy, on [−R,R]m×[t0,T][-R,R]^{m}\times[t_{0},T],

‖F⁡(z,t)−F⁡(z′,t′)‖2⩽Lz​‖z−z′‖2+Lt​|t−t′|.\displaystyle\|F(z,t)-F(z^{\prime},t^{\prime})\|_{2}\leqslant L_{z}\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}+L_{t}|t-t^{\prime}|.

sup(z,t)∈[−R,R]m×[t0,T]‖F⁡(z,t)‖2⩽K0.\displaystyle\sup_{(z,t)\in[-R,R]^{m}\times[t_{0},T]}\|F(z,t)\|_{2}\leqslant K_{0}.

Then for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exist architecture parameters

L,M,J,K,κ,γ,γt\displaystyle L,M,J,K,\kappa,\gamma,\gamma_{t}

chosen by the constructive approximation scheme in the proof of Theorem 1 of [CHZW23], with the replacements

d↦m,1+β↦Lz,τ↦Lt,R↦R,\displaystyle d\mapsto m,\qquad 1+\beta\mapsto L_{z},\qquad\tau\mapsto L_{t},\qquad R\mapsto R,

and a ReLU network

such that

sup(z,t)∈[−R,R]m×[t0,T]‖fθ​(z,t)−F⁡(z,t)‖∞⩽ϵ.\displaystyle\sup_{(z,t)\in[-R,R]^{m}\times[t_{0},T]}\|f_{\theta}(z,t)-F(z,t)\|_{\infty}\leqslant\epsilon.

Moreover,

supz∈ℝm,t∈[t0,T]‖fθ​(z,t)‖2⩽C​K0.\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\,t\in[t_{0},T]}\|f_{\theta}(z,t)\|_{2}\leqslant CK_{0}.

Proof. [Proof of Proposition 6] Using PW⟂=ID−PWP_{W}^{\perp}=I_{D}-P_{W}, we have

‖PW⟂​Ai‖F2=Tr⁡(Ai⊤​PW⟂​Ai)=di−Tr⁡(W⊤​Ai​Ai⊤​W).\displaystyle\|P_{W}^{\perp}A_{i}\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(A_{i}^{\top}P_{W}^{\perp}A_{i})=d_{i}-\operatorname{Tr}(W^{\top}A_{i}A_{i}^{\top}W).

Therefore

Γk​(W)\displaystyle\Gamma_{k}(W) OPEN=ω1​c1​d1+ω2​c2​d2−Tr⁡(W⊤​Mmix​WCLOSE).\displaystyle=\omega_{1}c_{1}d_{1}+\omega_{2}c_{2}d_{2}-\operatorname{Tr}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(W^{\top}M_{\rm mix}W}}\right).

Since

Tr⁡(Mmix)=ω1​c1​d1+ω2​c2​d2,\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(M_{\rm mix})=\omega_{1}c_{1}d_{1}+\omega_{2}c_{2}d_{2},

minimizing Γk​(W)\Gamma_{k}(W) is equivalent to maximizing

Tr⁡(W⊤​Mmix​W)\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(W^{\top}M_{\rm mix}W)

over all D×kD\times k matrices with orthonormal columns. By the Rayleigh–Ritz variational principle, the maximum equals

∑j=1kλj​(Mmix),\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}(M_{\rm mix}),

and it is achieved by taking WW to be the top kk eigenvectors of MmixM_{\rm mix}. The monotonicity in kk follows immediately from the eigenvalue formula. Finally, the residual is zero if and only if PW⟂​A1=0P_{W}^{\perp}A_{1}=0 and PW⟂​A2=0P_{W}^{\perp}A_{2}=0, which is equivalent to both component subspaces being contained in span⁡(W)\operatorname{span}(W). ∎

Corollary 11 (Principal-angle interpretation).

Let Ai∈ℝD×diA_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{i}} have orthonormal columns for i=1,2i=1,2. Set

a:=ω1​c1,b:=ω2​c2,Mmix:=a​A1​A1⊤+b​A2​A2⊤.\displaystyle a:=\omega_{1}c_{1},\qquad b:=\omega_{2}c_{2},\qquad M_{\rm mix}:=aA_{1}A_{1}^{\top}+bA_{2}A_{2}^{\top}.

Let r:=min⁡{d1,d2}r:=\min\{d_{1},d_{2}\}, and let

0⩽φ1⩽⋯⩽φr⩽π/2\displaystyle 0\leqslant\varphi_{1}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant\varphi_{r}\leqslant\pi/2

be the principal angles between span⁡(A1)\operatorname{span}(A_{1}) and span⁡(A2)\operatorname{span}(A_{2}). Then MmixM_{\rm mix} is zero on

OPEN(span⁡(A1)+span⁡(A2)CLOSE)⟂.\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\operatorname{span}(A_{1})+\operatorname{span}(A_{2})}}\right)^{\perp}.

On the two-dimensional principal-angle block associated with φj\varphi_{j}, the eigenvalues of MmixM_{\rm mix} are

λj±=a+b2±12(a−b)2+4​a​b​cos2⁡φj,j=1,…,r.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{\pm}=\frac{a+b}{2}\pm\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(a-b)^{2}+4ab\cos^{2}\varphi_{j}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,r. (C.9)

If d1>d2d_{1}>d_{2}, then MmixM_{\rm mix} has additionally d1−d2d_{1}-d_{2} eigenvalues equal to aa. If d2>d1d_{2}>d_{1}, then MmixM_{\rm mix} has additionally d2−d1d_{2}-d_{1} eigenvalues equal to bb. All remaining eigenvalues are zero.

Proof. [Proof of Corollary 11] By the cosine-sine decomposition for two subspaces, there exist orthonormal principal vectors uj∈span⁡(A1)u_{j}\in\operatorname{span}(A_{1}) and vj∈span⁡(A2)v_{j}\in\operatorname{span}(A_{2}) such that uj⊤​vj=cos⁡φju_{j}^{\top}v_{j}=\cos\varphi_{j} for j=1,…,rj=1,\ldots,r. The action of PA1P_{A_{1}} and PA2P_{A_{2}} decomposes into independent principal-angle blocks, together with the extra directions belonging only to the larger subspace.

On the block spanned by uju_{j} and the normalized component of vjv_{j} orthogonal to uju_{j}, the matrix a​PA1+b​PA2aP_{A_{1}}+bP_{A_{2}} has trace a+ba+b and determinant a​b​sin2⁡φjab\sin^{2}\varphi_{j}. Hence its two eigenvalues are

λj±=a+b2±12​(a+b)2−4​a​b​sin2⁡φj=a+b2±12​(a−b)2+4​a​b​cos2⁡φj.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{\pm}=\frac{a+b}{2}\pm\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(a+b)^{2}-4ab\sin^{2}\varphi_{j}}=\frac{a+b}{2}\pm\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(a-b)^{2}+4ab\cos^{2}\varphi_{j}}.

If d1>d2d_{1}>d_{2}, the d1−d2d_{1}-d_{2} directions in span⁡(A1)\operatorname{span}(A_{1}) orthogonal to span⁡(A2)\operatorname{span}(A_{2}) are eigenvectors with eigenvalue aa. If d2>d1d_{2}>d_{1}, the additional directions in span⁡(A2)\operatorname{span}(A_{2}) have eigenvalue bb. On the orthogonal complement of span⁡(A1)+span⁡(A2)\operatorname{span}(A_{1})+\operatorname{span}(A_{2}), both projectors vanish, so the eigenvalue is zero. ∎

In the special case d1=d2=dd_{1}=d_{2}=d, c1=c2=1c_{1}=c_{2}=1, and ω1=π,ω2=1−π\omega_{1}=\pi,\omega_{2}=1-\pi, we have a=πa=\pi and b=1−πb=1-\pi, so (C.9) becomes

λj±=12[1±1−4​π​(1−π)​sin2⁡φj],j=1,…,d.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[1\pm\sqrt{1-4\pi(1-\pi)\sin^{2}\varphi_{j}}}}\right],\qquad j=1,\ldots,d. (C.10)

In the balanced case π=1/2\pi=1/2, this further reduces to

λj±=1±cos⁡φj2.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{\pm}=\frac{1\pm\cos\varphi_{j}}{2}.

Consequently, the optimal kk-dimensional shared projector in Proposition 6 selects the directions corresponding to the largest eigenvalues of MmixM_{\rm mix}. Principal directions with small angles concentrate most of their mixed subspace energy in one direction, whereas directions with large angles require additional latent dimensions to be well represented. If φj=0\varphi_{j}=0, then λj−=0\lambda_{j}^{-}=0, reflecting that the corresponding principal-angle block degenerates into a shared one-dimensional direction.

Proof. [Proof of Theorem 7] Score structure under mixed training. Let

pmix:=ω1​p1+ω2​p2,ω1+ω2=1,\displaystyle p_{\rm mix}:=\omega_{1}p_{1}+\omega_{2}p_{2},\qquad\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}=1,

and denote by pmix,tp_{{\rm mix},t} the corresponding forward-diffused density. Since the forward diffusion is linear,

pmix,t​(x)=ω1​p1,t​(x)+ω2​p2,t​(x).\displaystyle p_{{\rm mix},t}(x)=\omega_{1}p_{1,t}(x)+\omega_{2}p_{2,t}(x).

𝒰mix​(U)=𝒪mix​(U)+ℐmix​(U),\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\rm mix}(U)=\mathcal{O}_{\rm mix}(U)+\mathcal{I}_{\rm mix}(U),

Comparison between U=V1U=V_{1} and U=WkU=W_{k}. The preceding bounds make explicit how the projector choice affects the regularity of the projected mixed comparator. If U=V1U=V_{1} and V1V_{1} is well aligned with A1A_{1}, then H1​(V1)=V1⊤​A1H_{1}(V_{1})=V_{1}^{\top}A_{1} is well conditioned, and Lψ,1​(V1)L_{\psi,1}(V_{1}) is moderate. However, if A2A_{2} is far from the source subspace, then H2​(V1)=V1⊤​A2H_{2}(V_{1})=V_{1}^{\top}A_{2} may be rank deficient or ill conditioned. In that case, the component-2 comparator can suffer from large reconstruction error, and the regularity constant Lψ,2​(V1)L_{\psi,2}(V_{1}) may deteriorate through ‖H2​(V1)†‖op\|H_{2}(V_{1})^{\dagger}\|_{\rm op}.

By contrast, WkW_{k} is chosen to reduce the joint subspace residual

Γk​(W)=ω1​c1​‖PW⟂​A1‖F2+ω2​c2​‖PW⟂​A2‖F2.\displaystyle\Gamma_{k}(W)=\omega_{1}c_{1}\|P_{W}^{\perp}A_{1}\|_{F}^{2}+\omega_{2}c_{2}\|P_{W}^{\perp}A_{2}\|_{F}^{2}.

When kk is large enough for WkW_{k} to capture the important directions of both A1A_{1} and A2A_{2}, the matrices Hi​(Wk)=Wk⊤​AiH_{i}(W_{k})=W_{k}^{\top}A_{i} are better conditioned, reducing the component-comparator constants Lψ,i​(Wk)L_{\psi,i}(W_{k}) and the component reconstruction part of ℐmix​(Wk)\mathcal{I}_{\rm mix}(W_{k}). In the ideal case where span⁡(Ai)⊆span⁡(Wk)\operatorname{span}(A_{i})\subseteq\operatorname{span}(W_{k}), all nonzero singular values of Hi​(Wk)H_{i}(W_{k}) equal one, and the componentwise spatial regularity reduces to the intrinsic constant βi+1\beta_{i}+1.

However, the posterior-weight regularity constants Lπ,Wk​(R)L_{\pi,W_{k}}(R) and τπ,Wk​(R)\tau_{\pi,W_{k}}(R) are controlled by the projected densities qi,Wk,tq_{i,W_{k},t}. These constants need not improve monotonically with kk: a higher-dimensional projection may preserve more information for distinguishing the two components, but it may also create sharper posterior transitions or smaller projected-density lower bounds on a fixed box. Therefore, the main guaranteed benefit of WkW_{k} is the reduction of the joint structural residual and the potential improvement of component reconstruction conditioning, while the posterior-compression and dimension-dependent statistical costs must be tracked separately. ∎
